title: Nauseated Face Emoji 🤢 Meaning: Gross, Sick or Cringe
description: The nauseated face emoji 🤢 is green and means queasy, disgusted or grossed out. Learn how real nausea differs from “ew” reactions, and how it compares with 🤮.
summary: The 🤢 nauseated face means something is making the sender feel sick. That can be literal, like motion sickness, food poisoning or a hangover, or a reaction of disgust to a smell, a sight, an idea or a person's behavior. It says ew in a single character.
meaning: Turning green is an old cartoon sign for feeling ill, and 🤢 uses it without any subtlety. The bulging cheeks and pinched eyes show someone trying to keep their lunch down. In its literal sense people send it from the back seat of a winding car ride, on a rough ferry, after questionable seafood or during the queasy early weeks of pregnancy.

Far more often it is a judgment. 🤢 is the standard reply to anything revolting: a photo of mold, a description of a medical procedure, pineapple on pizza if you feel strongly about it. It also covers moral or social disgust. Someone hearing about a creepy message, a cheating ex or an overly sweet public display of affection might answer with nothing else.

Younger users lean on it for cringe. A secondhand-embarrassing video, an old photo of yourself or a try-hard caption gets 🤢 to mean that made me physically uncomfortable. In this use it is frequently exaggerated and affectionate, especially between friends teasing each other about crushes or couples who are being too cute.

It can be aimed at people in a hurtful way, and that deserves care. Posting 🤢 under someone's selfie or about how they look is a direct insult. The emoji has no gentle reading when a person's appearance is the subject, which is why it shows up in bullying as well as banter.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Most uses are quick reactions. A friend describes what they found in the office fridge and you send 🤢. It also explains why you are quiet or leaving early, as in feeling 🤢 after the bus ride. One emoji generally means disgust; a longer message around it usually means real nausea.

contexts.label: On TikTok and Instagram
contexts.body: Comment sections use it to rate anything unpleasant, from food combinations to bad behavior in a storytime video. It is also a staple of jokes about couples, where single viewers comment 🤢 under romantic content to mean you two are sickeningly sweet, generally without real hostility.

contexts.label: From a friend or sibling
contexts.body: Between people who are close it is almost always teasing. Tell your sister about your date and she may reply 🤢 simply because hearing about your love life is her idea of too much information. It signals mock horror, not real disapproval.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: It is tolerable for clearly shared annoyances, such as the state of the microwave, in a casual channel. Using it about a proposal, a client or a coworker's lunch is rude. For actual illness, a plain note that you feel sick is clearer and more professional.

examples.text: The milk expired two weeks ago and I already drank some 🤢
examples.meaning: Real queasiness and regret after consuming something spoiled.

examples.meaning: Disgust at someone's creepy or inappropriate behavior.

examples.meaning: Cringing hard at their own past self.
A strong dislike of a particular food.

combos.meaning: Disgust escalating from queasy to actually throwing up, used for emphasis.
Carsick, or dreading a long and twisting drive.
Awkward and gross at once; a reaction to cringe-inducing content.
Hungover, or swearing off a drink that caused last night's trouble.

confusedWith.difference: 🤮 is past the point of holding it in and is actively throwing up. It is the stronger, cruder choice. 🤢 is the warning stage, so it suits mild disgust and real nausea that has not peaked.
😷 mainly means illness or precaution and only hints at blocking a bad smell. 🤢 is unmistakable revulsion. Choose the mask for a cold and the green face for anything that turns your stomach.
🥴 is dizzy, tipsy or dazed, with a wobbly smile. It feels off balance rather than sick. 🤢 comes later in the night, when the room has stopped being fun.

avoid: Never post it about a person's body, face or photo unless you intend to insult them.
Do not use it to react to food someone made for you or food from another culture.
Avoid it in response to someone's sincere confession or vulnerable news.
design: A face tinted green, with furrowed brows, squinting or anxious eyes and a tight, wavy mouth, often with puffed cheeks as though holding back vomit. Every major platform uses green, though the shade runs from yellow-green to a deep sickly tone. Some versions are green all over and others fade from green at the top to yellow below.

faqs.q: What does 🤢 mean from a girl or a guy?
faqs.a: It means the same from anyone: disgust or nausea. If it is a reply to something you said, they found it gross, cringe or too much, possibly as a joke. If they send it about themselves, they probably feel unwell. Tone depends on how close you are.

It can be. Directed at a person, their looks or their work, it is plainly insulting. Directed at a situation, a smell or the sender's own stomach, it is just descriptive. Among friends it is often used in exaggerated fun.

Intensity. The nauseated face feels sick; the vomiting face is being sick. People often use 🤢 for something mildly gross and save 🤮 for the truly revolting, or send both in a row to show the reaction getting worse.

faqs.q: Why is the nauseated face green?
faqs.a: Green skin is a long-standing visual shorthand in comics and animation for nausea, echoing the English expression of looking green around the gills. The emoji follows that convention so the feeling is obvious at a glance, even at very small sizes.
